item.description: arXiv:2605.07775v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Balancing exploration with exploitation is a core challenge in black-box optimization and reinforcement learning. We introduce POETS ($\textbf{Po}$licy $\textbf{E}$nsembles for $\textbf{T}$hompson $\textbf{S}$ampling), a novel framework that bridges uncertainty quantification and policy optimization. Our approach is grounded in the insight that policies trained with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization implicitly encode an underlying reward function. Building on this, POETS bypasses the complex, nested process of training an uncertainty-aware reward model and separately fitting a policy to this model. Instead, we directly train a policy ensemble to capture epistemic uncertainty by matching implicitly encoded reward functions to online, bootstrapped data. To overcome the prohibitive compute and memory constraints of ensembling Large Language Models (LLMs), POETS utilizes an efficient architecture: the ensemble shares a pre-trained backbone while maintaining diversity through independent Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) branches. Theoretically, we show that POETS implicitly approximates KL-regularized Thompson sampling, a principled optimization strategy with optimal cumulative regret bounds of $O(\sqrt{T \gamma_T})$. Empirically, we demonstrate that POETS achieves state-of-the-art sample efficiency across diverse scientific discovery domains, including protein search, therapeutic molecular design, and quantum circuit design. POETS also improves the optimization trajectory and out-of-distribution transfer of reinforcement learning across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, proving particularly robust in off-policy settings with experience replay or in small dataset regimes.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Menet, Andreas Krause, Abbas Rahimi

item.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.16757v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent language systems are often built as hand-designed workflows, where agents are assigned semantic roles and communication protocols are specified in advance. We propose NeuroMAS, a method that first treats a multi-agent language system as a trainable and scalable neural-network-like architecture with LLM agents as nodes and intermediate textual signals as edges. In NeuroMAS, agent nodes are role-free but structure-aware: the topology only determines how information can flow in general, while reinforcement learning training determines how nodes communicate, specialize, and coordinate. This formulation shifts multi-agent design from workflow engineering toward architecture design, where depth, width, connectivity, and growth protocol become scalable sources of capability. Further, we provide a theoretical perspective showing why such modular textual computation is more parameter-efficient when tasks admit hierarchical decompositions. Experiments show that NeuroMAS improves significantly over both inference-time and trained multi-agent baselines. We further find that organizational scaling is path-dependent: larger systems can be challenging to train from scratch, but become feasible when grown progressively from smaller trained systems. These results suggest that learned neural multi-agent systems are a promising scaling axis for LLMs.

item.title: Transient Amplification in Cascaded Gradient Methods: Exact Minimax Laws and Tracking without Resonance
item.description: arXiv:2606.04031v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Leader-follower gradient iterations, including bilevel and two-time-scale methods, can exhibit large finite-time excursions despite asymptotic stability. For cascaded iterations with block matrix J = [[A,0],[C,D]], symmetric diagonal blocks of norm at most gamma < 1, and coupling norm at most c, we prove an exact, dimension-free minimax formula: at every horizon t, the worst-case amplification equals the spectral norm of [[gamma^t,0],[c t gamma^(t-1),gamma^t]], attained by an aligned two-dimensional quadratic. Consequently, the worst transient is on the order of 1 + c/(1-gamma), and eigenvalues alone cannot predict finite-time gain. Under martingale noise, the aligned system has stationary follower variance sigma^2 c^2 (1+gamma^2)/(1-gamma^2)^3, establishing cubic inverse-gap scaling. For quadratic followers, the coupling is linked to follower sensitivity R by C = (I-D)R. When the leader is isotropic and the follower map is positive semidefinite, amplification is at most 1 plus the operator norm of R, independently of the spectral gaps. A look-ahead Newton update eliminates follower memory and is minimax-optimal among linear updates that track the leader exactly. Experiments validate the bounds and show that accelerated or inexact follower solvers can exceed the sensitivity bound when their effective maps have negative eigenvalues. Code and experiment scripts: https://github.com/Axym-Labs/transient-amplification
item.dc:creator: Ahanaf Hasan Ariq, Davide Wiest

item.title: Online Distributional Prediction via Latent Cluster Geometry Under Drift and Corruption
item.description: arXiv:2606.18778v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Online learning in non-stationary streams is often formulated as tracking a point estimate, although many applications require predicting the full data-generating distribution. We study online distributional prediction under drift and bounded causal adversarial corruption. Candidate laws are represented by variable-size latent cluster configurations that induce predictive distributions. A Gibbs quasi-posterior over configurations yields an online predictor by posterior averaging and can be sampled using reversible-jump MCMC. The method uses no stream likelihood but specifies a kernel-mixture predictive family. We evaluate cumulative Wasserstein-1 regret against the time-varying true law and study periodic restart, sliding-window, and exponential-discounting memory against full history. The bounds separate PAC-Bayesian complexity, corruption-sensitive posterior perturbation, and drift through $A_T^{\mathrm{OT}}=\sum_{t=2}^T W_2^2(p_{t-1}^*,p_t^*)$. Under bounded support, latent quadratic growth, predictive-map regularity, and localized-comparator assumptions, restart has sublinear high-probability cumulative regret when $0\le a<1$, $q,\zeta,b<1$, $0\le\gamma<\beta<1$, and $0<h<(1-a)/2$. Here $a,q,\zeta,b$ control the polynomial growth of drift, predictive-family approximation error, off-order posterior mass, and oracle-order switch cost; $\lambda_s\asymp s^{-\beta}$ and $H\asymp T^h$. Corruptions satisfy the segment-local condition $\Lambda_{r,s}=O(s^\gamma)$, so a sublinear global budget alone is insufficient. The regime requires oracle-informed tuning, $\varepsilon_T=o(1)$, and fixed confidence or $\log(1/\delta_0)=T^{o(1)}$. Sliding-window and discounted guarantees additionally require the stated localized-memory condition.
item.dc:creator: Navyansh Mahla, Prateek Chanda, Ganesh Ramakrishnan

item.title: Discretization and Statistical Consistency of Functional Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2608.04531v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Functional flow matching learns to generate random functions, such as velocity fields or solutions of partial differential equations, by continuously transforming a simple probability distribution into a target distribution. In practice, however, training and sampling use only finitely many grid values or coefficients. Does refining these observations recover the intended function-space model, and how do observation, learning, and numerical errors affect the generated distribution? We address these questions by first proving that the velocity targets used for training converge in mean square when the finite reconstructions converge to the underlying functions and remain uniformly bounded. The observations need not be nested: each refinement may replace earlier sensor locations. We also give quantitative bounds for orthogonal projections and extend the result to point observations under suitable regularity and reconstruction assumptions. We then bound the discrepancy between the generated and target distributions in Wasserstein distance, separating observation, learning, numerical, and endpoint errors without requiring uniqueness of the population finite-dimensional dynamics. For a normalized quadrature neural operator representing the learned velocity field, we establish stability and learning bounds with constants independent of the number of sensors. Under fixed model dimension and boundedness assumptions, the statistical excess risk decreases at an inverse-sample-size rate, up to logarithmic factors. A Gaussian example combines these estimates into an explicit sampling-error rate.
item.dc:creator: Lennon J. Shikhman

item.title: Verdict Instability of OOD Scores under Reference Resampling
item.description: arXiv:2609.00691v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Post-hoc out-of-distribution detectors are fitted on a finite reference set, so every score they produce is an estimate. If we had chosen a different set, some verdicts would have moved. We measure that movement by resampling the reference set and recording the bootstrap standard deviation of the score, which we call verdict instability. It admits a closed form with no fitted parameters. The instability of a verdict is the within-class dispersion of the assigned class along the query's direction, divided by the square root of that class's reference count. That count is what separates verdict instability from the geometry of the score distribution, and it is identifiable only under class imbalance. Instability grows with the local dispersion. Far-OOD queries lie along the low-variance directions of an anisotropic embedding, so the distance-based scores in common use assign their highest values to the verdicts that are most reproducible. Only estimators of local dispersion carry the sign a practitioner expects. We give a rule that predicts this sign for any score from a single label-free correlation, and abstention driven by a wrong-signed score turns out worse than abstention at random on every dataset we test.
item.dc:creator: Donghoon Lee, Shinjin Kang

item.title: Bandits with Probing: Optimal Coverage and the Role of Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2609.15248v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In bandits with probing, a learner selects at most $k$ of $n$ arms per round, earns the largest of their rewards, and competes with the best fixed single arm. For independent arms with i.i.d. rewards in $[0,1]$ and $2\le k<n$, the minimax regret is $\Theta\bigl(\frac{n-k}{n}\min\{T,n/k\}\bigr)$, the cost of locating an unknown good arm, and observing only the maximum suffices to attain it. In particular, two probes give $\Theta(\min\{T,n\})$ regret, which resolves two open questions of Bhaskara et al. (2023) with weaker feedback. Our policy turns the probing surplus, the excess of the maximum over each probed arm, into exploration capital, and a permanent random core yields the sharp dependence on $k$. On arbitrary fixed reward arrays, same-round contrasts between blocks of arms attain the same rate, because the surplus pays for the stability of mirror descent. Winner feedback, the maximum together with its winning label, instead incurs an additional learning cost under joint i.i.d. rewards and on fixed arrays. We characterize this cost even when values are revealed only intermittently, using policies that know neither the horizon nor the revelation rate. For three independent arms and two probes, exact maxima, Bernoulli-rounded maxima with winning labels, and winning labels alone have minimax regret $\Theta(1)$, $\Theta(\sqrt T)$, and $\Theta(T)$: rounding preserves conditional means but not the rate.
item.dc:creator: Yongjie Guan

item.title: SOL: Measuring Gaps between Text Distributions by Double Sliced Wasserstein Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.06513v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Evaluating text generation requires measuring how well the generated distribution matches the data distribution. For autoregressive models, this is done by the perplexity. Diffusion and flow-based language models can only provide a likelihood bound, whose tightness differs between model families. Sample-based substitutes such as generative perplexity with entropy do not consider the distribution fit. We propose SOL, a distance between text distributions. Each sequence is represented by the empirical measure of its hidden states under a fixed transformer and the distributions of these measures are compared by the double sliced Wasserstein distance. We prove that SOL is a metric if the transformer is injective. Experiments show that SOL detects distributional failures, recovers expected model trends, and provides stable sample-based estimates. We put forward SOL to fill the gap in the current evaluation protocol used for non auto-regressive models. As a first step we use SOL to re-evaluate a variety of models trained on OpenWebText.
item.dc:creator: Gregor Kornhardt, Moritz Piening, Jannis Chemseddine, Gabriele Steidl

item.title: SpectrumQuant: Spectrum Alignment for LLM Quantization
item.description: arXiv:2610.20303v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Orthogonal transforms have emerged as an effective tool for low-bit quantization of large language models (LLMs), as they reshape activation distributions without changing the underlying model function. Existing approaches typically rely either on fixed data-agnostic transforms, such as Hadamard rotations, or on calibration-time optimization of learned rotations. We study rotation selection from first principles and show that maximizing covariance leads to spectral alignment and provides a principled criterion for constructing quantization-friendly orthogonal transforms. Based on this insight, we propose SpectrumQuant, a closed-form rotation method that estimates activation covariance from calibration data and uses it to construct a covariance-aware orthogonal transform for post-training quantization. Our formulation characterizes quantization-friendly rotations as compositions of alignment and mixing components, while recovering Hadamard matrices as a special case. Interestingly, a class of butterfly matrices belongs to this category. In the realm of LLM quantization, SpectrumQuant bridges the gap between data-agnostic structured rotations and learned rotations, providing an effective and efficient data-aware alternative for post-training quantization. Experiments on Llama and Mistral models show that SpectrumQuant is competitive with state-of-the-art rotation strategies while requiring less than one-third of the GPU memory and significantly less time than learned rotations approaches like SpinQuant and DartQuant.
item.dc:creator: Dwaipayan Haldar, Indranil Patra, Azhar Yousuf, Chandra Sekhar Seelamantula

item.title: Privacy Accounting for Empirical Denoisers
item.description: arXiv:2610.27710v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as the foundation of modern generative systems, yet their high memorization capacity raises privacy concerns. While differentially private (DP) training provides formal guarantees, it comes at a cost in sample quality. In this work, we study a complementary question: how much privacy loss is incurred during the sampling process itself? Directly analyzing modern neural denoisers is challenging because their sensitivity to a single training example is generally intractable. To overcome this challenge, we construct and analyze a clipped privacy-accountable empirical denoiser, a training-free estimator of the Bayes-optimal denoiser, whose per-step sensitivity can be computed explicitly, allowing each denoising step to be a Gaussian mechanism. This perspective enables privacy accounting under Gaussian DP when each training example contributes to each denoising step, and under $f$-DP trade-off functions when each generated sample uses a single randomly subsampled block of the training data. We report every $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ guarantee as a certified upper bound from a privacy loss distribution accountant, and use a cumulant-based Edgeworth approximation as a fast diagnostic, characterizing where it is reliable and where it becomes anti-conservative. We also analyze the privacy loss along the denoising trajectory and show that it grows steeply near the critical window in which semantic content is formed. This observation motivates hybrid samplers that use the private empirical denoiser through the formative steps where it remains a faithful proxy for the neural denoiser, then switch to a public neural denoiser for the remaining refinement. Our results on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64 show that the privacy of diffusion models depends not only on the training procedure, but also on sampling-time design choices such as subsampling, stopping time, and hybrid denoising.
item.dc:creator: William Cheng, Dongjun Kim, Mijung Park

item.title: SABLE: Scalable Affine Bayesian Latent-space Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2610.31495v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Complex objects such as engineering designs and proteins are often difficult to optimise because their design spaces exhibit high-dimensional structure and objective evaluations are expensive. Generative models provide continuous latent representations, but their latent spaces can have thousands to tens of thousands of dimensions, creating a regime where the latent dimension $D$ greatly exceeds the evaluation budget. We introduce SABLE, a Bayesian optimisation method for high-dimensional latent spaces with an isotropic distribution and limited budget. SABLE uses a Bayesian affine surrogate for prediction and acquisition, treating higher-order structure as surrogate discrepancy. After $N$ observations, the slope update has dimension at most $N-1$, yielding a decomposition of each query into an in-span component optimised by expected improvement (EI) in at most $N$ dimensions and an off-span component governed by a scalar norm. We show that the off-span norm implicitly selected by affine EI can lead to underexploration, and SABLE instead prescribes it using a finite-horizon schedule, without restricting search to a learned subspace. A recompression scheme reduces information to $\mathcal O(M)$ pseudo-observations, bounding refitting cost by $\mathcal O(M^2D+M^3)$ while keeping parameter inference, prediction, and acquisition decisions to tens of milliseconds. Across synthetic benchmarks and latent-space optimisation tasks, SABLE achieves high sample efficiency and reduces decision time by several orders of magnitude at large budgets.
item.dc:creator: Erik Bodin, Lisa Maria Kreusser, Donney Fan, Henry Moss, Geoff Pleiss, Nicolas Durrande
